newsitem.title: UK: Reports suggest softer UK inflation target to come.
newsitem.headline: Reports suggest softer UK inflation target to come.

text.p: Britain's Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown looks set to keep the 2.5 percent inflation target but drop the words "or less', opting for a symmetrical point target carrying penalties for undershooting as well as overshooting.

The Financial Times and two other newspapers said on Thursday that in his Mansion House speech later today, Brown will impose penalties on the Bank if it misses the 2.5 percent target by 1.0 percent on either side.

"If this is correct, the new target will be slightly easier to hit than the old one," said Michael Saunders, UK economist at Salomon Brothers. "Effectively the Chancellor is aiming for a slightly looser target."

The Treasury declined to comment on the report, which said each time inflation is above or below the target by one percent Governor of the Bank of England Eddie George would have to write an open letter to Brown explaining why.
The FT added that the letter would have to say what actions the Bank is taking to correct it and predict when inflation will be back on track.

The current system states that inflation should be 2.5 percent or less, so is "biased down". The Bank misses the target if underlying inflation is, for example, 0.25 percent above the trget, but hits it if inflation is 0.25 percent below.

"With the suggested new remit, the Bank would probably aim for a central inflation forecast of 2.5 percent, slightly higher than the level the Bank would aim for under the existing target, which probably amounted to an implicit target of 2.0 to 2.5 percent," said Saunders.

Ian Stewart, UK economist at Merrill Lynch, agreed the report suggests a clear softening of policy. "This represents a diminution of the toughness of monetary policy. The current target, effectively a band between zero and 2.5 percent, is bring replaced by a higher band of 1.5 to 3.5 percent."
He said this means the government is not prepared to tolerate inflation below 1.5 percent, but it is prepared to tolerate it between 2.5 and 3.5 percent.
And he questioned the timing of the change.

"It is rather strange to soften the inflation target at this stage of the experiment," said Stewart, referring to the Bank of England's new powers to set interest rates, granted to it only weeks five weeks ago.
"It would have been more sensible to try and build credibility in the new system."
The newly empowered Bank raised interest rates at the first opportunity, by a quarter point last Friday, so has already won some anti-inflationary spurs.
Michael Dicks, UK economist at Lehman Brothers, said the Bank will probably now go out of its way to emphasise it is aiming for inflation at 2.5 percent and not just the top of the wider band.
"If this is the new target, I think it will go down very badly in financial markets," said Dicks.
He said the suggested band is implying that the costs of having inflation under 1.5 percent are the same as the costs of it above 3.5 percent.
"That is clearly not the case and it will make for a very poor comparison with other European economies," said Dicks.
UK government bonds shrugged off the reports and were firm on Thursday morning. The September future was up 6/32 at 113-25.
